Dark Matter on Trial

Cold and warm dark matter universes grown from the same initial ripples in a 2D model universe, searched for subhalos, populated with galaxies, and compared with a mock satellite survey drawn from the cold universe. After an expert review and a full re-analysis: warm dark matter with the largest half-mode mass cuts resolved subhalos per Milky Way analog from — to —. In 2D the cutoff is sharper and sits at lower mass than in 3D, and it does not line up with 3D even in units of fluctuation strength. A conservative bound from the simulations themselves survives; the emulator-based bound does not.

Re-run with corrected code

  • The cold and warmest universes were simulated again after they turned out to predate a GPU fix (their early particle displacements differed from the current code by 6.8% and 38% rms). The two milder warm universes were already clean. Every number on this page now comes from the corrected set.
  • The science quantities barely moved. Comparing the re-runs with the originals, halo counts, subhalos per host, the warm/cold satellite ratio and the suppression scale all agree within their errors. Only the largest-scale power spectrum differed.
  • Runs are reproducible statistically, not bit for bit. The short-range force sums particles within a cell in a varying order, so roundoff differs from run to run. A deterministic ordering will be added after the convergence suite; a repeat run is measuring the resulting noise floor.

After the expert review

  • Hosts are now matched by shared particles. Each cold host is paired with the warm host holding most of the same particles, instead of by position. Pairing rates are in the table below; the warmest universe pairs fewer hosts because many of them genuinely merged or changed.
  • Fits start above the completeness limit of — particle masses, found by rerunning the finder at stricter settings and at half resolution. A conservative 400-particle cut gives a consistent suppression scale.
  • The subhalo finder now uses the simulation's real softening. It had been 14× too large, which hid most subhalos. Satellite counts carry about ±10% from the 2D binding-energy reference, included as a systematic.
  • Suppression is compared with 3D in σ(M) as well as mass. The two do not agree, so this experiment makes no claim about 3D suppression amplitudes.
  • The emulator bound is withdrawn. It fails the closure test for the Mhm 300 universe. The bound shown is built directly from the simulations, capped so that warm predictions never exceed cold ones.
  • Fake fragments checked. Lovell-style cleaning, now applied to subhalos too, flags only objects below the completeness limit; the fits do not change.

The two mildest warm universes hold about 6–9% more resolved subhalos than the cold one around matched hosts. No suppression function can reproduce an excess, which is why the emulator fails closure for one of them and why the bound caps warm predictions at the cold ones.

Convergence

Each variant changes one setting from the main run and repeats the cold and warmest universes. Values are variant ÷ main run; a quantity counts as converged within 10% or 2σ. A repeat of the main settings gives the run-to-run noise floor, and a second seed shows cosmic variance rather than numerical error. Verdict: halo counts, subhalos per host and the warm/cold satellite ratio are converged in particle number, mesh, softening and timestep. The suppression scale M50 shifts by about 20% when the softening is doubled, so it carries that as a systematic. Single power-spectrum bins at the smallest or largest scales are the only other outliers, from coarser mesh smoothing and cosmic variance.

Method and caveats

Simulations: periodic 2D comoving particle-mesh runs (6144² particles, 4096² mesh) with a Gaussian-split short-range force on an RTX 5080, Zel'dovich initial conditions with identical random phases in every model, and a comoving KDK leapfrog. Warm dark matter uses the Viel et al. (2005) transfer function, labelled by its half-mode wavenumber; Mhm is defined on a disc, the 2D analogue of the usual sphere.

Structure: friends-of-friends hosts, a 2D SUBFIND port with gravitational unbinding in the log potential and the simulation's own softening, and merger trees across 16 snapshots. Hosts are matched across universes by shared particle IDs; Milky Way analogs are the 30 most massive cold hosts and their matched counterparts.

Galaxies: a 2D adaptation of Nadler et al. (2020), with luminosity from peak mass, a reionization threshold in peak velocity, and orphan galaxies after disruption. The bound uses the simulations directly; the fitted-suppression emulator is reported only through its closure test.

Limits of this work: it is a 2D model universe. Gravity in 2D has no escape speed and no natural halo radius, so host radius and binding use conventions (50× mean density; binding measured against a reference radius). Suppression amplitudes do not transfer to 3D in mass or in σ(M). The convergence suite (second seed, 4× fewer particles, half-resolution mesh, double softening, half timestep, plus a repeat run) supports the main quantities; the suppression scale carries a ~20% softening systematic, and science runs use a single seed. Masses are in particle masses. 3D reference fits: Lovell et al. 2014, Lovell 2020b, and COZMIC I (Nadler et al. 2025).
